Two threads access the same memory location, at least one of the accesses writes, and nothing in the program orders one before the other. "Orders" is the technical part: a mutex, an atomic, starting or joining a thread all create that order, and plain code in two threads does not. A program with a data race has undefined behaviour for its whole execution, and not merely at that line (

c.v: You pass with the definition including the word "ordered", the right prediction for the counter, two fixes with their costs, and three of the four cases in 4. Calling the counter "a bug that shows up under load" without naming undefined behaviour is a partial pass. Saying that two threads writing different elements of a vector race is a fail, because it would push you towards locking things that need no lock.
A thread is a flow of execution inside a process that runs its own function while sharing the process's memory with every other thread. In C++20 you start one with
, which takes a callable and its arguments, runs it, and in its destructor asks it to stop and waits for it to finish, which is called joining.

Sharing memory is what makes threads fast and what makes them dangerous. A data race is two threads reaching the same memory location, at least one of them writing, with nothing ordering the two accesses; a program containing one has undefined behaviour. The everyday symptom is a lost update.

reads, adds and writes, so when both threads read 41, both write 42 and one count is gone. I ran a two-thread counter with 400000 increments ten times and it finished between 200000 and 257328, never at 400000.

The mechanism that fixes it is a mutex, short for mutual exclusion: an object that one thread at a time can own. A thread that asks for a locked mutex waits until the owner releases it, and the release also publishes everything that thread wrote, so the next owner sees it. You never call

, which locks in its constructor and unlocks in its destructor, so every return and every exception unlocks. The mutex lives in the same class as the data it protects, and every access to that data, reads included, holds it.

What it costs is throughput and a new failure mode. Those same 1000000 increments took 53 ms through one mutex and 1 ms when each thread counted into a local and merged once at the end, so the cheapest concurrency is the kind that shares nothing. The failure mode is deadlock: two threads that take two mutexes in opposite orders wait for each other forever, which
prevents by taking both in one step.
In the robot you meet this wherever a callback thread and a control loop share state: the newest scan, an odometry accumulator, a queue of commands.

A program contains a data race when two accesses to the same memory location happen in different threads, at least one of them is a write, neither is atomic, and neither happens before the other (

Two words in that definition carry the weight. A

c.v: reporting that it had to kill the program. Nothing was printed, no sanitizer said a word, and neither AddressSanitizer nor UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer has anything to say about deadlock: the program is doing exactly what it was told. This is the failure mode that reaches production, because a deadlock needs an interleaving that a short test rarely produces.
The fix is one line, and the rule behind it is

blocks.text: 40000 moves in both directions: left 1000, right 1000, sum 2000

c.v: locks all of its mutexes with an algorithm that cannot deadlock: it takes one, tries the rest, and on a failure releases everything and starts again from the one that refused. Forty thousand moves in opposite directions finish in 20 milliseconds. The alternative, when the mutexes cannot be taken together, is a lock order that the whole program agrees on, written down and checked in review: always the sensor before the map, always the map before the log. That leaves the tool. ThreadSanitizer instruments every memory access and every synchronisation operation, builds the happens-before graph at run time, and reports accesses that are not ordered. It cannot be combined with AddressSanitizer, which this curriculum's flags use, and GCC refuses the pair outright:
. So a race hunt is its own build:

blocks.text:
g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -g -fsanitize=thread racy_counter.cpp -o racy_counter
# In WSL, ThreadSanitizer needs address space layout randomisation switched off:
setarch $(uname -m) -R ./racy_counter

c.v: Three things in that report are worth reading twice. It names both accesses, the read and the write that raced with it, with the thread that did each. It names the location, here a variable on the main thread's stack, which is

. And that particular run printed 400000, the correct answer: TSan slows every access down enough that the increments happened to interleave cleanly. The tool finds the race, not the wrong answer, and that is exactly why it is worth running. The same program built with the mutex runs clean under TSan and exits with 0.
TSan's cost is a slowdown of roughly 5 to 15 times and 5 to 10 times the memory, so it goes in a nightly job or a targeted test rather than in every build (
, whose figures the GCC port shares). It reports only races on paths that actually run, so give it a test that starts several threads and exercises the shared object. And it understands
and thread creation, so correct locking silences it rather than needing suppressions.
